title: What Time It Is at Boot: A Clock That Starts in 1970, the Jump When It Is Set, and Records That Sort Themselves Wrongly

questions.question: Which clock should every timeout and rate of the robot be measured in?
options: Time since boot, which only goes forward and cannot be set
The wall clock, which everyone agrees on
GPS time, which is the most accurate
Either, as long as it is used consistently
questions.explanation: The wall clock can be set forward or back at any moment. An interval measured on it jumps with it; time since boot cannot be set at all.

questions.question: The clock is set at 40 s on a boot that started in 1970. How big is the jump?
options: About 40 s, the time since boot
About 1.79e9 s, 56.9 years, in one step while 0.2 s of real time passed
An hour, the usual time zone error
Nothing: setting a clock is not a jump
questions.explanation: The wall clock went from 1970 to 2026 in one step. Anything timing itself on it saw 56.9 years pass in a fifth of a second.

questions.question: A timeout of 0.3 s is measured on the wall clock, and the clock is put back an hour. When does it fire?
options: At once, since an hour has passed
After 0.3 s, as designed
Never: the elapsed time is negative
After an hour and 0.3 s
questions.explanation: With the clock an hour back, now minus the last heartbeat is negative and never exceeds the timeout. Measured since boot it expired as it should.

questions.question: Sorted by the wall clock, how many of six records of two boots were in the wrong place?
options: 5: the early records of the second boot carry 1970 time and go before the whole of the first boot
None: the wall clock gives the true order
1, the record at the sync
All 6
questions.explanation: Boot 2's first records were written before its clock was set, so they carry 1970 and sort ahead of everything. Ordered by boot and time since boot, none is misplaced.

questions.question: Why does check_validity answer unknown before the clock is set?
options: Certificates cannot be checked without a network
It is quicker than comparing dates
The certificate's dates are in another time zone
A 1970 clock says not yet valid for a certificate that is fine
questions.explanation: A guess must not be used to say yes or no. On a 1970 clock a good certificate looks 56 years early. Saying unknown, and not yes or no, lets the robot fetch the time first.

questions.question: What does a robot that suspends do to the monotonic clock on many systems?
options: It resets it to zero
It makes it run faster to catch up
It does not count the suspended time
Nothing: it keeps counting
questions.explanation: Time since boot is shorter than the real time. On many systems the monotonic clock stops while the machine is suspended. A timeout measured across a suspend is then shorter than the real time that passed.
